archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (possession-first)
archetype.definition: A Penguins team that wins the 5-on-5 chance battle most nights but has lost the finishing, goaltending and close-game coin flips, so its 3-5-1 record understates how it is actually playing.

report.headline: The chances say playoff team; the finishing, saves and top line say otherwise
report.take:
Pittsburgh sits seventh in the Metropolitan at 3-5-1 and 25th on the site, and the pace line (64 standings points) looks like a lottery season. The process doesn't match that. A 54.1% 5-on-5 expected-goals share ranks 8th in the league and is the best mark in any of the five seasons in its history block, ahead of the 103-point 2021-22 team's 53.5%. The shot-attempt share is 11th. This team is pushing play. It just isn't being paid for it.

The gap shows up in conversion at both ends. Skaters are shooting .107, 20th, and the goalies are stopping .879, 22nd and well under the league's .893, so the all-situations PDO is 98.6 against a league average of 100.6. Pts vs Goal Diff is -1.9, 29th, which means the standings have been a bit harsher than even a -4 goal differential implies. Two caveats keep this from being pure bad luck. The goalies' combined GSAx is 0.7, roughly average, so Arturs Silovs and Sergei Murashov are mostly allowing what the shots deserve. And the team allows 27.6 shots a game, 22nd. Much of the damage is coming outside the 5-on-5 picture the xGF% describes.

The bigger thing the team numbers hide is who is driving them. The depth is winning: Connor Dewar and Blake Lizotte are both at 61.8% xGF, and Tommy Novak is at 55.6% with seven points. The minutes leaders are not. Rickard Rakell (0 goals on 21 shots), Sidney Crosby (-6) and Bryan Rust are all below 49%, and Erik Karlsson, the top-minute defenseman, is at 47.1% despite nine assists. Evgeni Malkin's five goals carry most of the scoring at the top, which is why the forward group grades a D while the blueline holds a B. Opponents' wingers are piling up points against this defense; that rank is 31st of 32, so the top-line matchups are getting beaten at both ends.

The direction is worrying in the short term. After the 7-0 opener in Philadelphia and an overtime win over Montreal, the last five went 1-3-1 with 20 goals allowed. The road trip ended with losses at Chicago, Colorado and Vegas. Nine games is a small sample and the shot-share base is real, so this should climb toward the middle of the conference. It won't be a playoff team, though, until the top six starts winning its minutes, not only scoring a few of them.

strengths.title: Wins the 5-on-5 chance battle
strengths.body: A 54.1% expected-goals share is top-ten and beats every season in the history block. It comes from structure as much as talent, so it should hold up better than shooting or save percentage. Over time, teams that out-chance opponents like this usually find their goal differential.

strengths.title: Depth centers tilting the ice
strengths.body: Dewar and Lizotte are both at 61.8% xGF in roughly 13 minutes a night, and Novak adds 55.6% with three power-play points. The bottom of the lineup is beating its matchups, which is unusual and valuable. The question is whether it lasts as opponents take those minutes more seriously.

strengths.title: A penalty kill above average
strengths.body: The kill is at 83.3%, 11th and well above the league's 79%, which has kept special teams from sinking the record. Last season's kill was 81.4%, so this is roughly in line with recent form rather than a fluke.

concerns.title: The top line is losing its minutes
concerns.body: Rakell, Crosby and Rust lead the forwards in ice time and all sit below a 49% xGF. Rakell has yet to score on 21 shots. Opponents' wingers are producing at a rate that ranks 31st, so the top matchups are bleeding at both ends. Rakell's shooting should turn, but the chance share is the real problem.

concerns.title: Save percentage near the bottom
concerns.body: The goalies are stopping .879 against a league .893, and the defense ranks 26th in goals allowed per game. Some of this is the volume and quality allowed beyond 5-on-5: the team-level GSAx is close to average, and Murashov's -1.4 is the only clearly negative number. Expect some recovery, but not a goaltending rescue.

concerns.title: Recent form sliding the wrong way
concerns.body: The last five games went 1-3-1 with 20 goals allowed, scoring down by about a goal a game against the season rate. That stretch was mostly on the road against strong Western teams, but the defensive leaks are consistent with the season-long shots-against problem.

trend.note: A 7-0 opener and an overtime win gave way to a 2-6 October, and the last five games were the worst stretch yet. The underlying shot share has held up even as the results slid.

weekAhead.headline: Two top-six teams, then a winnable Nashville game at home
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Utah against the site's 5th-ranked team. The Mammoth lead the league in fewest shots allowed (19.3 a game) and have the league's best power play. Florida, 6th on the site with a 58% shot-attempt share, comes to Pittsburgh next. Both opponents grade A or better on the blueline or near it and both out-chance teams at 5-on-5. Pittsburgh's main edge, winning the possession game, won't come easily in either.

Nashville to close the week is the opening. The Predators are 25th in xGF% and 27th in CF%, so this is the game where Pittsburgh's process should show up on the scoreboard. The catch is that Nashville's goaltending is stopping .906 and its power play is 4th. A split of the first two and a win on Saturday would be a decent week; anything less deepens the hole.

keyMatchups.title: Utah's power play against the kill
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts a league-best 35.3% of its power plays, and Pittsburgh's 83.3% kill is its best special-teams asset. Utah's own kill is 25th, so the penalty battle could swing that game in either direction. Discipline matters more than usual.

keyMatchups.title: Florida's possession versus Pittsburgh's
keyMatchups.body: Florida's 58% shot-attempt share ranks 3rd, ahead of Pittsburgh's 52%. This is the one opponent likely to take away the territorial edge the Penguins rely on. Whoever controls play here likely wins.

keyMatchups.title: Out-chancing a Nashville team built on saves
keyMatchups.body: Nashville is 25th in xGF% but sits 8th in save percentage. That is the mirror image of Pittsburgh: it is getting results its process doesn't earn. Pittsburgh should control the shots, and the game becomes a test of whether its finishing can beat a hot goalie.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Crosby-Rakell minutes finally win their matchups, or keep giving back what the depth lines create.

restOfSeason.body:
The 64-point pace won't hold. A top-ten expected-goals share combined with bottom-third shooting, saves and close-game luck is a profile that usually corrects, and the history block shows this core has posted 88 to 103 points in most recent seasons. Expect the shooting percentage to drift toward league average and the save percentage to recover somewhat, landing the team around 80 to 90 points. That is bubble territory in a division where Carolina and the Rangers are already ahead.

The ceiling depends on the top of the lineup. If the depth's chance share regresses before the top line's improves, the 54% share will slide toward the 51% of last season. Without last year's 101.2 PDO, that version of this team is closer to the 80-point 2024-25 club. The goaltending tandem looks average rather than bad, so there is no star-goalie upside to count on either.
swingFactors: Power play climbing toward league average

confidence.note: Nine games is a small sample, but the shot-share signal is strong.
